findings: Advanced HF remains a major cause of morbidity and mortality, with many patients failing optimized therapy and devices. Early recognition is difficult due to heterogeneous presentations. Standardized diagnostic criteria and dedicated care pathways are essential for timely management.
take_home: Early identification and structured care pathways are key to improving outcomes in advanced heart failure patients.

title: [Multimodality imaging in heart failure: phenotyping and clinical decision-making].
why: It shows how combining echo, CMR, CT and nuclear scans can give a complete picture of a heart failure patient, which is key for tailoring treatment in the ICU.
findings: Echocardiography is still first‑line but now includes strain, RV‑arterial coupling and congestion checks with lung and venous ultrasound. CMR is the gold standard for tissue characterization, especially fibrosis that predicts arrhythmia risk. CT maps coronary anatomy for procedures, while nuclear imaging reveals metabolism, inflammation and sympathetic tone. Integrating these tests, guided by the clinical question, lets clinicians track disease and adjust therapy.
take_home: Using a multimodality imaging toolbox gives the most accurate phenotyping and decision‑making in heart failure, improving patient care in the ICU.

title: [Ten questions about cardiogenetics].
why: Genetic testing refines diagnosis, predicts arrhythmic risk, and guides therapy in cardiomyopathies and channelopathies.
findings: The review outlines when to order testing, which genes to include, how to interpret results, the diagnostic and prognostic value of variants, their role in arrhythmic risk stratification, therapeutic decisions, and cascade family screening.
take_home: Integrating genetic data with phenotype, family history, and disease context is key for optimal patient management.

title: Genotype, Phenotypic Severity, and Survival in Pediatric Dilated Cardiomyopathy: A Report From the Pediatric Cardiomyopathy Registry.
why: Genetic testing in kids with DCM rarely changes prognosis or severity, so it shouldn’t drive treatment decisions.
findings: Only 19% of children had a pathogenic variant, higher in those over 12. Having a variant didn’t link to worse heart‑failure symptoms or outcomes, and those without a variant trended toward better echo recovery.
take_home: In pediatric DCM, genetics has low diagnostic yield and doesn’t predict severity or recovery, so focus on clinical management rather than genetic results.

title: Multi-institutional assessment of practice patterns in the use of cardiovascular magnetic resonance and computed tomography for pulmonary valve replacement planning: A survey-based study.
why: It shows how different centers approach imaging for pulmonary valve replacement, which can impact planning and outcomes.
findings: Most sites start with CMR and add CCT only for certain valves; CCT is used when pacemakers are present; functional CCT is common; measurement methods differ, with most using multiplanar reformats; only a minority use advanced techniques like 4D flow; reporting takes 60–120 minutes; 84% want a standardized protocol.
take_home: Standardizing imaging protocols for PVR planning could streamline workflow, reduce radiation, and improve consistency across centers.

title: Liver Extracellular Volume in Patients With Tricuspid Regurgitation: A Novel Prognostic Marker.
why: It shows that liver ECV measured by CMR can flag TR patients at higher risk of death or HF hospitalisation, adding value beyond conventional TR severity scores.
findings: Patients with high liver ECV had worse baseline right‑HF signs and a 2‑year higher rate of death or HF admission. In multivariable models, high liver ECV remained an independent predictor (HR 1.82). Liver ECV added prognostic information over the TRI‑SCORE.
take_home: Liver ECV on CMR is an independent, incremental marker of right‑HF risk in tricuspid regurgitation and can improve patient stratification.

title: Atrial Fibrillation Burden as an Outcome in Clinical Trials.
why: AF burden is becoming a key metric that could change how we design and interpret AF trials, which matters for both research and clinical practice.
findings: The review explains that AF burden—time spent in atrial fibrillation—captures more clinically relevant information than the traditional 30‑second episode rule. It highlights the need for standardized detection, definition, and analysis methods, and discusses how regulators are starting to consider AF burden as a primary endpoint.
take_home: AF burden offers a more sensitive and potentially regulatory‑friendly outcome for AF trials, but its adoption requires consensus on measurement and analysis standards.

title: Anatomical Insight Into Idiopathic Ventricular Arrhythmias Originating From the Papillary Muscles.
why: Knowing the anatomy of papillary muscles helps a cardiologist target ablation sites better and avoid complications.
findings: PAPs are anatomically distinct, causing inconsistent ECG patterns and varied VA morphologies. Imaging like ICE, CT, and CMR clarifies their structure and connections, explaining the electrophysiologic quirks.
take_home: A detailed anatomical and imaging assessment of papillary muscles is key to improving catheter ablation success for idiopathic ventricular arrhythmias.

title: Interpreting High-Sensitivity Cardiac Troponin in Clinical Practice and Emerging Directions: Detection Is No Longer Diagnosis.
why: Because troponin interpretation is key to distinguishing true myocardial infarction from non‑ischemic injury in the ICU setting.
findings: High‑sensitivity troponin detects myocardial injury in many conditions, but misclassification is common, leading to over‑diagnosis of MI. Accurate classification requires serial testing, guideline algorithms, and consideration of non‑ACS causes such as CKD, sepsis, arrhythmias, and takotsubo. Emerging troponin biology may eventually aid interpretation.
take_home: Clinicians must use context‑aware, serial testing and guideline‑endorsed algorithms to avoid over‑diagnosing MI and to properly risk‑stratify patients with troponin elevation.

title: Diastolic Dysfunction in Congenital Heart Disease: A Pressure-Volume Loop Analysis of Borderline Left Heart.
why: This study tells us that in children with borderline left heart, diastolic dysfunction is mainly due to stiff ventricles, not relaxation problems, so we should rethink our drug choices.
findings: They measured pressure‑volume loops in 13 bLV kids and 14 ccTGA kids. Relaxation indices were similar, but the bLV group had much higher passive stiffness constants. The end‑diastolic relationship was shifted upward and leftward in bLV.
take_home: Target therapies that reduce ventricular stiffness—like surgical fibroelastosis resection—may be more useful than lusitropic drugs in these patients.

title: Prediction of All-Cause Mortality, Cardiovascular Mortality, and Angiographic Coronary Disease From LVEF Reserve: Findings From the Multicenter REFINE PET Registry.
why: It shows that a simple measure from PET imaging—LVEF reserve—can flag patients at higher risk of death and complex coronary disease, which could influence how we triage and manage them.
findings: Patients with a negative LVEF reserve had a 38% higher risk of all‑cause death compared to those with a reserve above 5%. The lower the reserve, the steeper the mortality gradient. A negative reserve also correlated with left‑main and three‑vessel disease on angiography.
take_home: LVEF reserve from PET is a useful, non‑invasive marker that identifies patients who may need more aggressive coronary evaluation and closer follow‑up.

title: Cardiac Electrophysiological Impact of Sodium Glucose Cotransporter 2 Inhibitors: A Comprehensive Review.
why: SGLT2 inhibitors not only lower heart‑failure events but also seem to curb arrhythmias, which matters for ICU patients.
findings: They dampen sympathetic tone and boost parasympathetic activity, lowering atrial fibrillation and even sudden death in some trials. Meta‑analyses hint at a modest but consistent benefit. Preclinical work shows they block late sodium current and shift metabolism to ketones, while microRNAs linked to fibrosis are down‑regulated.
take_home: SGLT2 inhibitors could be a useful adjunct for arrhythmia prevention, but dedicated trials are needed to confirm causality and dose effects.

title: Multimodality Imaging for Left Atrial Appendage Closure: Practical Guidance Across Preprocedural, Intraprocedural, and Postprocedural Phases.
why: It gives a practical, phase‑based imaging roadmap for left‑atrial‑appendage closure, which is key for safe stroke prevention in AF patients who can’t anticoagulate.
findings: Transesophageal echo remains the gold standard for thrombus detection and guidance, while cardiac CT offers high‑resolution 3‑D sizing and leak assessment. Device‑specific rules differ for Watchman and Amulet, and standardized thrombus/leak classification can improve reproducibility. Emerging CT‑first workflows, 4‑D imaging, AI and computational modeling are pushing precision planning.
take_home: Adopt a multimodality, standardized imaging protocol—TEE for guidance, CT for sizing and leak, and consider AI or 4‑D tools—to enhance procedural safety and long‑term outcomes.

title: Right Atrial Phasic Function Improves CMR-Based Prognostication in Patients with Heart Failure with Mildly Reduced Ejection Fraction: A Multicenter Study.
why: RA strain adds prognostic info beyond standard imaging, helping risk stratify HFmrEF patients
findings: RA conduit strain independently predicts adverse outcomes; adding it to clinical and imaging variables boosts model C-index to ~0.80
take_home: RA conduit strain from CMR is a valuable incremental prognostic marker in HFmrEF

title: Prediction and Risk Stratification for 30-Day Mortality in Stable Acute Pulmonary Embolism: Recalibration of the Multimarker Calculator and Evaluation of the AHA/ACC Classification.
source: Eur Heart J Acute Cardiovasc Care
why: Even though it’s about PE, the new recalibrated multimarker calculator gives a more accurate 30‑day mortality estimate for stable patients, helping us decide who needs closer monitoring or early intervention.
findings: The multimarker calculator and the 7‑category AHA/ACC scheme outperformed the ESC model in discrimination. The original calculator over‑estimated risk, but after recalibration it better matched observed outcomes and identified a smaller high‑risk group. The simplified 3‑category AHA/ACC classification showed a clear stepwise increase in mortality across phenotypes.
take_home: Use the recalibrated multimarker calculator for precise 30‑day risk in stable PE, and the simplified AHA/ACC phenotype categories for quick risk grouping.

title: Variation in Pediatric Extracorporeal Cardiopulmonary Resuscitation Survival After In-Hospital Cardiac Arrest: Development and Validation of a Survival Model for Risk-Standardized Survival Rates: An Analysis of the Extracorporeal Life Support Organization Registry.
why: It shows that outcomes after pediatric ECPR vary a lot between hospitals, so we can benchmark and improve care.
findings: The model predicts survival with fair accuracy (AUC ~0.73 derivation, 0.68 validation) and is well calibrated. The median odds ratio of 1.30 indicates significant between‑hospital differences after adjusting for patient risk.
take_home: Risk‑adjusted survival rates highlight real inter‑hospital variation in pediatric ECPR outcomes, but the model isn’t ready for bedside decisions yet and needs external validation.

title: Traumatic Emergency Thoracotomy for Resuscitation in Shock (TETRiS): a national service evaluation of resuscitative thoracotomy practice outside the operating theatre.
why: Even though it’s trauma, the study shows that early, physiologically favorable intervention is the key to survival—principles that apply to any shock scenario in the ICU.
findings: Out of 116 patients, 43% achieved ROSC and only 7% survived to discharge. Survival was much higher in tamponade cases and when the procedure was done in the ED rather than prehospital. No one survived beyond 10 min of arrest.
take_home: Resuscitative thoracotomy is only lifesaving in a narrow window—tamponade and early, favorable physiology—so patient selection and timing are everything.

title: Great debate: a dual biomarker strategy improves the triage of patients with suspected acute coronary syndrome.
why: It discusses how adding copeptin to troponin could speed up ruling out MI, a key issue for ED flow and patient safety.
findings: The article reviews evidence that a dual biomarker approach may allow earlier safe discharge than the standard 0/1‑h or 0/2‑h troponin algorithms, but also highlights uncertainties and potential pitfalls.
take_home: Dual biomarkers look promising for faster triage, but until larger trials confirm safety, clinicians should use them cautiously and in context of current ESC guidelines.

title: Clopidogrel Versus Aspirin Monotherapy According to Atherothrombotic Risk Profile.
why: Clopidogrel monotherapy after DAPT may cut ischemic events in high‑risk PCI patients without extra bleeding, which matters for post‑PCI management.
findings: In patients with a high atherothrombotic risk, clopidogrel lowered major cardiac events compared with aspirin, while in low‑risk patients there was no difference. Bleeding rates were similar in both groups.
take_home: For high‑risk PCI patients, switch to clopidogrel monotherapy after DAPT to reduce ischemic events without increasing bleeding.

title: The Right Ventricle in Focus: State-of-the-Art CMR Imaging - Challenges, Standards, and Innovations.
why: This review gives a comprehensive overview of CMR techniques for the right ventricle, which is crucial for accurate assessment in many acute and chronic conditions that we manage in the ICU. Understanding these advances helps us interpret imaging reports and guide therapy decisions.
findings: CMR is the reference standard for RV volumes, function, flow, and tissue characterization. Key challenges include RV geometry, trabeculation, and thin wall. Current techniques include cine imaging, phase-contrast flow, late gadolinium enhancement, and emerging methods like 3D cine, 4D flow, parametric mapping, and novel reconstructions. These innovations improve accuracy and reproducibility.
take_home: CMR is rapidly evolving and becoming a precise, actionable tool for evaluating right ventricular disease, so staying current with its techniques will enhance our diagnostic and prognostic capabilities.

title: Impact of obesity on clinical outcomes and the treatment effect of catheter ablation in atrial fibrillation: insights from CABANA.
why: Obesity worsens AF burden and outcomes, so knowing its impact on ablation helps tailor therapy.
findings: In obese AF patients, ablation still cuts recurrence and improves symptoms, but they start with higher comorbidity and worse functional status. No BMI‑treatment interaction on the main composite endpoint, yet class II obesity patients had poorer absolute outcomes.
take_home: Catheter ablation remains effective in obese AF patients, but aggressive weight‑loss and comorbidity control are needed to improve their overall prognosis.

title: Impact of obesity on procedural safety and 1-year outcomes after pulsed-field ablation for atrial fibrillation.
why: It shows that obesity doesn’t raise procedural risk or long‑term recurrence after pulsed‑field AF ablation, so we can reassure obese patients.
findings: In a large nationwide cohort, higher BMI was linked to more advanced AF and larger ablation lesions, but periprocedural complications were low and similar across BMI groups. One‑year recurrence was driven by AF type, not BMI, with no significant difference between BMI <35 and ≥35.
take_home: Obesity does not worsen safety or long‑term success of pulsed‑field AF ablation, so we can proceed without extra caution for obese patients.

title: Performance of 0/1 h versus 0/3 h pathways in patients with suspected myocardial infarction: a systematic review and individual participant data meta-analysis of randomised controlled trials.
why: It tells us whether the faster 0/1‑hour rule‑in/out strategy changes safety or ED flow for MI patients, which is key for ED triage and guideline adherence.
findings: Across 110,933 presentations, the 0/1‑hour pathway had a slightly lower 30‑day death or type‑1 MI rate (0.8% vs 1.0%) but the difference was not statistically significant. Emergency department length of stay was essentially the same (about 314 vs 308 minutes).
take_home: The 0/1‑hour pathway is as safe and efficient as the 0/3‑hour approach—no clear advantage in outcomes or ED throughput.

title: A global men's health epidemiology within an intersectional framework.
why: It highlights that cardiovascular disease is a top killer for men, but the paper is broad and not specific to ICU practice.
findings: The review shows men die earlier mainly from non‑communicable diseases like heart disease and cancer, plus injuries, violence, and social factors. It stresses that biology and social determinants both shape male health outcomes.
take_home: Cardiovascular disease remains a leading cause of male mortality, but addressing social determinants is key to improving men's health overall.

title: Prone positioning and high-frequency oscillatory ventilation in early paediatric acute respiratory distress syndrome (PROSpect): an international, two-by-two factorial, response-adaptive, phase 3, randomised controlled trial.
why: Ventilation strategies can affect cardiac output and hemodynamics in the ICU, so knowing their impact helps us manage cardiogenic shock patients.
findings: The trial enrolled 424 children with moderate-to-severe ARDS. Prone positioning did not increase ventilator-free days compared to supine. High-frequency oscillatory ventilation also did not improve outcomes versus conventional ventilation. The study was stopped early for futility.
take_home: Prone positioning and HFOV offer no benefit in ventilator-free days for pediatric ARDS, so they should not change our ventilation approach.

title: Chlorhexidine within a standardized oral-care bundle for the prevention of ventilator-associated pneumonia: a pragmatic cluster-randomized crossover trial in six medical intensive care units.
why: Even though it’s not a cardiac study, ICU patients with cardiac disease often need ventilation, so VAP prevention matters for overall outcomes.
findings: The trial found no reduction in VAP incidence or 28‑day mortality when 0.12% chlorhexidine was added to a standard oral‑care bundle, and ICU length of stay was slightly longer in the chlorhexidine group.
take_home: Adding chlorhexidine to routine oral care in mixed medical ICUs does not improve VAP rates or survival and may modestly increase ICU stay.

title: Artificial Intelligence-Assisted, Electrocardiogram-Derived, Sequential Rule-Based Decision Tree for Exclusion of Acute Coronary Syndrome as the Etiology of Out-of-Hospital Cardiac Arrest: A Single-Center Retrospective Cohort Study.
why: It gives a quick, AI‑powered way to decide who really needs a cath lab after OHCA, which is a daily dilemma in the ICU.
findings: The rule‑based tree flagged about 50% of patients as ACS unlikely, with no missed ACS cases, especially in non‑shockable rhythms (AUROC 0.824). In shockable rhythms most stayed as potential ACS.
take_home: Use the AI ECG tree to safely rule out ACS in many post‑OHCA patients, but validate it prospectively before changing practice.

title: Ventilation Monitoring in Out-of-Hospital Cardiac Arrest Care.
why: Better ventilation during cardiac arrest could improve ROSC and survival, so we need tools that help EMS teams stick to guidelines.
findings: Using Real BVM Help, the proportion of ventilations within target rate rose from 48% to 74%, tidal volume from 15% to 45%, and both parameters together from 8% to 39%. ETCO2 monitoring alone was far less effective, with only 44% of breaths at target rate and 14% at target tidal volume.
take_home: Real‑time feedback devices like Real BVM Help markedly improve guideline‑concordant ventilation during out‑of‑hospital cardiac arrest.

title: Immunological signatures of sepsis in abdominal solid organ transplant recipients: A multilayer and multicentric prospective cohort study.
why: It shows transplant patients with sepsis survive better and have a distinct immune profile, which could affect ICU management of these patients.
findings: SOT patients had 84% vs 66% 30‑day survival, lower IL‑6/TNF‑α, higher IL‑18, preserved innate immunity with higher monocyte HLA‑DR, and distinct proteomic and metabolic signatures.
take_home: Abdominal transplant recipients with sepsis fare better and display a less inflammatory, more innate‑immune‑preserved phenotype, hinting at tailored ICU strategies.

title: Ventilator-associated pneumonia after traumatic brain injury: a timing-sensitive ecological framework of neuroimmune-pulmonary vulnerability.
why: It’s about ventilator‑associated pneumonia in TBI patients, not a cardiac condition, so it’s not directly relevant to your cardiology practice.
findings: VAP is common after TBI, clustering early and late, driven by early host vulnerability and later biofilm/multidrug‑resistant pathogens. It prolongs ventilation, ICU stay and antibiotics, but its independent mortality effect varies.
take_home: VAP after TBI is a timing‑sensitive interaction of ventilator exposure and early host vulnerability, not a distinct disease entity.

title: AI algorithms and external validation: promises, pitfalls, and a practical blueprint.
why: Because AI tools are becoming common in cardiology, and this paper outlines how to properly validate them so they actually work in real ICU settings.
findings: External validation on independent, representative data is the best way to estimate real-world performance. The authors list many pitfalls like hidden relatedness, spectrum bias, label noise, and analytic flexibility. They propose a blueprint: pre-register, use multi-site cohorts, avoid overlap, evaluate discrimination, calibration, net benefit, audit subgroups, document labeling, calculate sample size, and plan minimal updating.
take_home: Validate AI models rigorously with external, multi-site data and follow the authors’ blueprint before deploying them in patient care.

title: Systemic Hypertension and Survival in Pulmonary Hypertension.
why: Even though PH isn’t a core focus, understanding how systemic BP and heart rate affect survival can guide ICU management of these patients.
findings: Patients with pre‑existing hypertension and higher baseline systolic BP had a 26% lower mortality risk. Higher heart rate was linked to worse outcomes, and rising systolic BP during follow‑up was associated with better cardiac index and tricuspid function.
take_home: In pulmonary hypertension, higher systemic blood pressure and hypertension itself seem protective, while tachycardia and falling BP signal poorer prognosis.

title: N-Acetylgalactosamine-Conjugated Small Interfering RNA Targeting Hepatic Angiotensinogen in Hypertension: A Phase I Clinical Trial With Randomized Part A and Open-Label Part B.
why: Not directly relevant to cardiogenic shock or arrhythmias, but shows a novel antihypertensive approach.
findings: The GalNAc‑siRNA was well tolerated in healthy volunteers and hypertensive patients, with no serious adverse events. It dramatically lowered circulating angiotensinogen (≈90% reduction) and produced a modest 13‑mmHg drop in 24‑hour systolic BP after a single 600‑mg dose.
take_home: This phase‑I study demonstrates that AGT‑targeting siRNA is safe and can lower BP, but its clinical relevance for acute cardiac care remains limited.

title: Intensive vs More Intensive Lipid-Lowering Therapy and Plaque Regression in Statin-Naive Patients: Prespecified Analyses From the FLOWPROMOTE Randomized Clinical Trial.
why: It shows that a more aggressive statin/ezetimibe combo can shrink plaque faster in newly diagnosed CAD patients, which matters for prevention strategies.
findings: Patients on rosuvastatin plus ezetimibe had a 65% drop in LDL‑C versus 38% with atorvastatin alone. At 18 months, total plaque volume fell by 21% with the intensive combo versus 14% with atorvastatin, and non‑calcified plaque fell by 28% versus 20%.
take_home: For statin‑naive stable CAD, a more intensive lipid‑lowering regimen produces significantly greater plaque regression than a standard high‑dose statin alone.

title: Assessment of Ototoxicity in Patients With Heart Failure Receiving High-Dose IV Loop Diuretics.
why: Loop diuretics are a cornerstone of HF therapy, and this study shows high doses don’t raise ototoxicity risk, so we can push diuresis with confidence.
findings: In two small prospective cohorts, high‑dose IV loop diuretics rarely caused permanent hearing loss; temporary shifts were infrequent and resolved within hours; no dose‑response relationship was seen.
take_home: High‑dose IV loop diuretics are safe from an ototoxicity standpoint in heart‑failure patients.

title: Intersection of Patient and Hospital Rurality in Heart Failure Care and Outcomes.
why: Rural patients with HFrEF get less cardiology input and guideline therapy, leading to worse outcomes—something we need to address in our ICU practice.
findings: Rural patients treated in rural hospitals were less likely to receive cardiology consults and had lower rates of β‑blocker, ARNI, MRA, and SGLT2I use. They also had higher 1‑year readmission and mortality compared with rural patients in urban hospitals. Urban patients in rural hospitals fared worse than those in urban hospitals.
take_home: Improve access to cardiology consultation and guideline‑directed therapy for rural HFrEF patients to reduce disparities in outcomes.

title: Early Identification of Recurrent Out-of-hospital Cardiac Arrest Using Clinical ECG Features.
why: It shows that simple ECG metrics can flag impending rearrest, which is crucial in the ICU setting.
findings: In 1,298 ROSC patients, 40.7% had rearrest. Those who rearrested had lower heart rate, wider QRS, and higher heart‑rate variability. The best prediction (AUROC 0.74) occurred 1 minute before rearrest.
take_home: Monitoring ECG variability and QRS width could help anticipate rearrest and prompt earlier intervention.
